messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel, a 38-year-old European American high school teacher, described the mugging as the moment his ordinary sense of safety split open. It happened on an early winter evening after he left a grocery store near his home, carrying a bag of food and walking to his car in the lot. Two men came up fast from between parked vehicles, one crowding his shoulder while the other barked at him to hand over his wallet. Daniel remembered the metallic taste in his mouth when one of them shoved him against the car and he caught the smell of cold pavement, exhaust, and his own fear. In the weeks that followed, the memory would not stay in the past; when it broke through, it arrived with such force that it felt completely real across all his senses at once, and he could taste that same metallic edge as if he were back in the lot. He said it often forced its way into his mind when he did not want it to, especially when something around him resembled the scene enough to open the door.

Crowded places became the clearest and most painful reminder. The packed supermarket aisle, the school hallway between classes, and especially the crush of parents at basketball games could pull him straight back into that evening, and once the memory surfaced, it seemed to bring the whole event with it. Daniel found that after a vivid surge of reliving, he became convinced that the world was a dangerous place and that what had happened to him was deeply unfair, made worse by the belief that the people or institutions that should have protected him let him down. He felt angry that nothing had been done about it in any meaningful way, and that sense of injustice fed the memory itself; the more he dwelt on how wrong it was, the more the event seemed to reassert itself with the same taste, the same fear, the same helplessness. Even driving with other people could set this off, because being trapped in a car with someone else nearby reminded him of how vulnerable he had felt pinned in the lot, and from there the same thoughts about danger and abandonment returned.

Once the memory had taken hold, Daniel became intensely watchful. He studied people’s faces and body language to detect if they were a threat, scanning the expressions of strangers in the grocery store checkout line and the posture of men walking too close on the sidewalk. He scanned exits as soon as he entered any room or building, as if every classroom, restaurant, or church hall needed a quick map in case he had to get out. Unexpected movement nearby caused him to react as if he were in danger; a student reaching suddenly across a desk, a person turning quickly in a crowded corridor, even a car door slamming in the parking lot could make him jerk and brace himself. That constant vigilance seemed to confirm his worst assumptions. Because he was always checking for signs of threat, he found more moments that looked unsafe, and each one strengthened his belief that the world was dangerous and that no one could be counted on to keep him safe. The fear also pushed his attention back toward the memory, which returned more readily when he was already keyed up.

As his threat monitoring narrowed his life, the triggers multiplied. The crowded places he once moved through without thought now felt loaded with potential danger, and the first sign of bodies pressing too close would send him back into the memory and the anger attached to it. Loud noises carried similar force. The bang of a dropped binder in his classroom, a truck backfiring near the school entrance, or a sudden shout in a crowded corridor could make him jump hard enough that students noticed. After each startle, he was left more convinced that he had to keep scanning, which made him even more alert to faces, exits, and movement. Daniel had begun taking longer routes through the building to avoid hallways at passing time, and he chose to drive alone whenever he could; when he had to carpool with a colleague for an evening event, he sat rigidly, watching mirrors and shoulders instead of talking. Over months, those habits narrowed his teaching life and made him quieter at home, where his wife noticed that he seemed to arrive carrying an invisible tension.

By the time he sought help, Daniel felt worn down by the loop between what he remembered, what he feared, and what he could no longer ignore. He came in because he was exhausted by the constant sense that danger was lurking in ordinary places, and because he did not want his world to keep shrinking around crowded rooms, loud sounds, and every sudden movement. What frightened him most was the suspicion that if he stopped scanning, he would be caught off guard again; what he hoped for, though he could barely say it without feeling foolish, was to walk into a room, hear a noise, or sit in a car with other people without instantly feeling that same old mugging closing in on him.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows triggers leading to re-experiencing the memory, but it does not clearly state that triggers drive Daniel’s negative appraisals or beliefs.
It describes negative beliefs after reliving, but does not show those appraisals causing the memory to return.
It shows triggers bring back the memory, but not that the memory itself creates or generates new triggers.
The vignette shows threat monitoring reinforcing danger beliefs, but not that perceived threat directly leads to negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
It shows threat monitoring and scanning for danger, but not that threat directly produces specific triggers or reminders.
